articles.title: Croydon woman had no hot water or heating for most of pregnancy
articles.summary: Residents living in flats in Croydon are in limbo having have been without gas since March.
articles.body:
Samantha Banner and her partner have been living without heating or hot water for most of her pregnancy, relying on washing in buckets filled with kettle-boiled water, camping showers, or travelling elsewhere.

The couple are leaseholders of a flat at Admiral Court in Croydon, south London, where residents across the mixed-tenure development have been without a gas supply since 4 March due to "potentially dangerous leaks".

They say they've been caught up in layers of bureaucracy among the freeholder, the housing association, managing agents and the developer over who is responsible for the cost of remedial works, making it "hard to get answers."

With the original developer having gone into liquidation, the dispute over who should pay has left residents in the 65 flats facing uncertainty over whether the cost of replacing the pipework could ultimately fall on them.

Samantha, who discovered she was pregnant at the start of January, says the situation has made everyday life "extremely difficult".

For months, the couple were unable to shower at home, although they now have a camping shower involving a "big bucket of water that we fill up with a kettle, and have a really quick shower".

They were also preparing to exchange and move to a bigger family home when their buyer pulled out due to a combination of increased service charges and ongoing gas problems.

"We are in absolute limbo. We can't put it back on the market because of the situation with the gas."

She says there is still no clear time frame for the gas to be restored.

"It's going to be expensive, I get it, but no-one is claiming any liability on it. We're just left waiting for them to make their decisions."

Samantha isn't the only resident who feels trapped and unable to sell.

Zainab Ottun is a shared owner who was among the first residents to move into the building when it was completed in 2019.

She bought a 25% share of her £310,000 property, expecting it to be a "stepping stone" towards buying a larger home, but instead "it's not sellable".

She says there have been multiple gas leaks over the years, with the supply repeatedly cut off and reinstated as "weaknesses in the infrastructure were detected".

When the gas was switched off in March, Zainab was recovering from Achilles surgery and using crutches. Without hot water, she had to wash using a bucket.

"You don't buy a new build expecting it to crumble right before your eyes as you're living in it."

Akira Pascall, a paediatric nurse, is another resident of the block and lives with her partner and three-year-old son in a shared ownership flat.

The family initially boiled kettles to fill up buckets to wash and clean the dishes, but they've now invested in a camping shower.

"After long shifts you have to come home and fill up the shower. Work is stressful enough and you want to come home to a safe haven.

"You can't have people to stay. It takes so long to get ready. Three-year-olds are messy and you just want to stick them in the bath sometimes," she says.

Pascall is also angry that it's been suggested that residents may have to fund the cost.

"This is meant to be affordable housing. If we had that much money to re-pipe a building we would build our own block of flats," she says.

In August 2026, five months after the gas was switched off, an expert witness report commissioned by the freeholder, Groundinvest 101 (Limited), and managing agent Warwick Estates found that the gas supply pipework "has not been installed in compliance" with the standards set by the Institution of Gas Engineers and Managers (Igem).

The freeholder has now contacted a number of companies it says are "associated" with the original developer seeking to recover the cost of the remedial work.

The building was initially developed in 2019 by company UK Land Assets, which has since been liquidated.

The managing agent, Warwick Estates, says neither it "nor the freeholder" was involved with this development until some time after "substandard construction work" was originally carried out.

It says while "our foremost concern" is the residents, "significant obstacles... have led to delays in remediation".

It claims that under the terms of the lease, gas pipes "fall to the direct responsibility of the individual leaseholders", but "we and the freeholder appreciate that it is not a simple case of advising the leaseholders to raise their own claims or arrange their own repairs".

It adds that the defects are not covered by the building's warranty.

"We are now seeking further expert advice regarding the potential installation of electric heating and hot water for each flat. We are hopeful that this advice together with costs will be available in the coming weeks."

Leaseholders charity, the Leasehold Knowledge Partnership, believes there are "too many" similar cases, where taking legal action against the developer becomes difficult, if not impossible.

Martin Boyd, from the charity, says that since the Grenfell fire, it has become clear that "the law is still stacked against the leaseholders who have a limited means of redress for building defects".

This includes not having the "legal right to survey the building when they buy, so they have no means of knowing if a site has problems", he explains.

The charity has called on the government to strengthen the warranty schemes on new developments.

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government said: "The situation at Admiral Court is completely unacceptable and we strongly urge those responsible to carry out vital building works urgently.

"Through our Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill, we are going further to strengthen protections for leaseholders, including making commonhold the default tenure for new flats – giving people full ownership and control over their buildings from the outset."

'I'm still paying a mortgage for a home destroyed by a fire'

'I lost thousands in savings and my partner's money is in limbo'

The 'constant fear' of living in an overheated home with a baby

A spokesperson for Croydon Churches Housing Association (CCHA), which is the leaseholder of 22 apartments at Admiral Court, claims the freeholder is "responsible for identifying and implementing an effective long-term solution".

CCHA says it has been in regular contact with the freeholder and managing agent, and has pressed for urgent action and clarity on when heating and hot water will be restored.

In the meantime, CCHA says it has moved some tenants into alternative accommodation, provided electric heaters to all residents and offered temporary electric showers.

Shared ownership leaseholders have also received vouchers for essential items, with CCHA offering to cover additional electricity costs.

The BBC contacted Grangeford Asset Management, which manages the freehold and the company that built the flats, Cube Construction, for comment.

For residents like Samantha there is still no clear timetable for when the issues might be resolved.

articles.title: AfD’s victory tests Germany’s ‘firewall’ against the far right
articles.summary: Europe News: Numbers Not Enough To Form Govt; Talks On With Others To Gain MajorityBerlin: Alternative for Germany, or AfD, has established itself as a significant.
articles.body: Numbers Not Enough To Form Govt; Talks On With Others To Gain MajorityBerlin: Alternative for Germany, or AfD, has established itself as a significant political force in the 13 years since its founding, but it has never been part of any state or federal govt. That’s a result of what is often called a “firewall” against cooperation with the anti-immigrant, far-right party.That firewall faces its biggest test after AfD won a landslide victory in Sunday’s election in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt. AfD fell just short of an absolute majority, with 39 of 83 seats in the regional legislature. It won 43.8% of the vote, more than double its showing five years ago in the state, while Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s centre-right Christian Democrats lost about half its support.Germany’s mainstream parties have long said they would not work with AfD, which is classified by Germany’s domestic intelligence agency as an extremist group in some regions of the country — including the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. Any dealing by mainstream parties with AfD is particularly sensitive in view of Germany’s Nazi past.The AfD candidate for governor, Ulrich Siegmund, aims to become the first far-right head of a state govt and has said he will reach out to all other parties and individual lawmakers to assemble a governing majority. The far-left BSW reaffirmed its readiness to play kingmaker after it cleared the 5% threshold to enter Saxony-Anhalt’s state parliament.In addition to their hostility towards Germany’s political establishment and their social conservatism, the two parties share a number of priorities, including a hostility to mass migration — which BSW says harms local workers’ rights — suspicion of the mainstream media and a desire to end financial and military support for Ukraine and restore ties with Russia.“We’ve made no secret from the beginning that we’ll talk with all parties. AfD is part of that,” Thomas Schulze, BSW party’s lead candidate in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, said on Monday. Schulze said the mainstream parties’ refusal to work with AfD was “undemocratic”.Many Germans had believed their country had developed an immunity to nationalism and assertions of racial superiority after confronting the horrors of its Nazi past through education and laws to outlaw persecution.But as it turns out, that conviction was mistaken, and, similar to voters elsewhere, voters in Germany are increasingly empowering the extreme far-right party. AfD has rejected any accusations of being undemocratic and has repeatedly pushed back against the firewall. The firewall taboo has sometimes forced other parties into unusual alliances to keep AfD out of power.In Germany’s election last year, AfD achieved the best performance by a far-right party since World War II and became the strongest political force in parts of the country. AfD became the biggest opposition party in parliament after Merz’s party upheld the firewall and formed an unpopular coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats.Forming a govt that excludes AfD would only be possible if all the other parties that were elected worked together — CDU, Social Democrats, the Greens, the Left Party, and BSW. However, a coalition involving five partners would be unusual, very complicated and prone to instability.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: ‘Defend workplaces’: Protesting robots take to Warsaw streets to demand AI regulation
articles.summary: Europe News: Waving flags, “chanting” slogans and marching in circles: around 30 robots took to the streets of Warsaw on Monday to campaign for AI regulation in fr.
articles.body: Waving flags, “chanting” slogans and marching in circles: around 30 robots took to the streets of Warsaw on Monday to campaign for AI regulation in front of the Polish digital affairs ministry. The protest was organised by Democratism, an initiative that, according to its website, aims to launch debate “on how AI and robotisation affect the labour market”.“The robots present here are meant to show that this technology is already a reality,” Agibot A3, one of the AI-powered humanoid robots, said.Chants of “Defend workplaces”, “Time for rules” and “Don’t wait, regulate” played on loudspeakers as the robots — which ranged from bipedal humanoids to dog-like quadrupeds — demonstrated. “We particularly want to address the issue of the potential replacement of people both by humanoid robots and by artificial intelligence in cognitive work,” organiser Grzegorz Kulis said. “If we don’t react now, we may soon have a problem,” he added, emphasising the need for “rules and regulations that would serve as a shield protecting workers”.Aside from attracting the attention of several passers-by, Kulis said the use of robots was meant to show their existing capabilities and thereby the urgency of the situation. “These robots can already move around freely, they’re already ‘protesting’,” he said.The marching robots were met with a visit from Poland’s digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski, who spoke to Kulis on site. “Uncontrolled (AI) models, implemented into humanoids that will also keep evolving as robotisation moves forward, are a major problem,” Gawkowski said.Kulis, who is now the CIO of a robotics company and CEO of an employment agency, served two terms on the Labor Market Council at the ministry of family, labour and social policy. “We feel responsible for starting to inform society about the rapid and dynamic technological changes which personally frighten us,” he told AFP.In July, Poland’s conservative-nationalist president Karol Nawrocki signed into law a bill put forth by the ministry putting the EU’s AI Act into practice. It created an authority capable of enforcing existing EU regulations, which had already formally come into force.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Soon, Aussies could opt out of social media algorithms
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Australians could be given the option of opting out of powerful social media algorithms under new legislation cracking down on big tech, a minister sa.
articles.body: Australians could be given the option of opting out of powerful social media algorithms under new legislation cracking down on big tech, a minister said Monday. The draft law requiring a “digital duty of care” is expected to be introduced to Australia’s parliament this week.It would require firms like Meta to give users the option of turning off algorithms that tailor recommendations to their personal taste.“A lot of Australians appreciate the algorithm, both for the enjoyment they get out of it or the utility they get out of it,” communications minister Anika Wells told national broadcaster ABC. “A lot of Australians will want to choose the algorithm -- but we think that big tech should offer them the choice in the first place, and they should respect that choice.”“We should give Australians more choice over what they should see on their feeds,” she said.Social media firms have long faced scrutiny over their use of allegedly addictive algorithms and stand accused of directing users to sensational or extreme content to keep them scrolling. Australia implemented legislation barring children from social media platforms in Dec, part of a world-first crackdown designed to protect children from online bullying and “predatory algorithms”.The UK, France and others have followed suit. Data last month found that under-16s in Australia were increasing their use of social m­e­dia apps such as Instagram and TikTok despite the ban.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Maharashtra minister Nitesh Rane expressed support for the Vishva Hindu Parishad's (VHP) call to bar Muslims from the Navratri events in the state, alleging that otherwise this would lead to an increase in "love jihad" cases.Attendees at such festivities should undergo identity checks and recite the Hanuman Chalisa before entry, the BJP leader told PTI Videos on Monday."Love jihad" is a term used by right-wing activists to allege a ploy by Muslim men to lure women (mostly from the Hindu community) into relationships for religious conversion."Those who do not follow idol worship should not participate in Hindu religious events. Those coming for garba should show their identity and chant the Hanuman Chalisa before being allowed entry," Rane said, extending support to the VHP's demand.The VHP last week announced that Muslims "would not be allowed" entry to garba and dandiya venues across the state during the upcoming Navratri festival, and issued "guidelines" for organisers to verify participants' identities by checking their Aadhaar cards and applying tilak on their foreheads.The Navratri festival will begin on October 11.On the demand to curb DJ sound systems during the upcoming Ganesh festival, Rane called for the rules to be applied uniformly to all religious processions.“If DJs are not permitted during Ganesh festival celebrations, similar restrictions should apply to Eid processions as well,” he said.Rane alleged that loud music was played late into the night during recent Eid processions, adding that Hindus follow court orders and noise regulations.He also slammed Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) chief Raj Thackeray over his reported remarks about alleged vulgar dances during Kanwar Yatra events in parts of Uttar Pradesh, questioning why criticism was directed only at Hindu practices while statements by Muslim clerics were not similarly discussed.The BJP minister asserted that some people were attempting to "defame" Hinduism and Sanatan Dharma.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: EU debate takes shape as Macron backs under-15 social media ban
articles.summary: Europe News: France is preparing a second attempt at restricting social media for children under 15 while President Emmanuel Macron presses Brussels to turn the sa.
articles.body: France is preparing a second attempt at restricting social media for children under 15 while President Emmanuel Macron presses Brussels to turn the same age limit into a common European rule.He made the EU push in an August 29 letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, calling for a new "European legislative text" to "protect all children in the Union". The request came after France's Constitutional Council stopped the country's planned restrictions before they could take effect on September 1.Macron seeks one age limit across EUIn his letter, Macron told von der Leyen that it was now "essential to go further" and harmonise the under-15 restriction through European legislation. He has also sought support among EU countries for a common "digital majority", although governments differ over the age at which unrestricted social media access should begin, AFP reported. Von der Leyen has said Europe should consider "phased and gradual access for different age ranges".Recommendations presented to the Commission would impose the tightest controls on children under 13 and allow broader access as they get older, provided platforms meet safety requirements. Nearly two-thirds of respondents to a recent EU survey backed age-based restrictions on children's social media access, according to the European Commission.Court blocked French ban before September rolloutFrance's parliament had backed restrictions barring children under 15 from social media from September 1. The Constitutional Council struck down the relevant provisions on August 14, meaning the ban never came into force.The proposed rules would also have required age verification and the closure of existing accounts belonging to users below the threshold. The council found the blanket restriction disproportionate, saying it did not sufficiently distinguish between platforms according to the risks they posed or between children based on factors including age, maturity and family circumstances. It also raised concerns over safeguards governing age verification and personal data, Reuters reported.The ruling nevertheless left room for another attempt. The council recognised protecting children's best interests as a legitimate constitutional objective, and Macron has said he hopes to "find a way forward" through a narrower measure that complies with both EU law and the French Constitution.His August 29 letter followed that ruling, taking the campaign to the European level even as France began work on a revised national text.High school phone restrictions take effectA separate French measure restricting mobile phone use in schools did take effect with the start of the 2026-27 academic year. Rules already applied in primary and middle schools were extended to high schools from September 1, according to the French education ministry.While visiting Lycée Chaptal in Mende that day, Macron defended the measure, telling pupils that using a phone at school was "not compatible with paying attention in classes". He said the problem extended to adults, adding that attendees at some Elysée meetings were now asked to surrender their phones to prevent them from checking the devices during discussions.The school collected pupils' phones in numbered compartments during the visit. Reactions were mixed, with some students accepting the restriction and others describing it as "infantilising". Teachers' unions have questioned how rapidly schools can put the rules into practice.He also used the visit to return to social media access for minors. "This creates addictions and dependencies. It also leads to attention disorders," Macron told pupils. He added that heavier exposure to screens and social networks made it harder to sustain attention and concentrate on reading.France is now expected to produce revised national legislation in the coming months, while the European Commission prepares its own proposals following the expert panel's recommendations.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2004, Toronto began using cold water from 83 metres beneath Lake Ontario to cool downtown buildings; today the system serves 200 buildings across 40 million sq ft
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Deep beneath the surface of Lake Ontario, a layer of naturally cold water has become an unlikely part of Toronto’s urban infrastructure. Instead of re.
articles.body: Deep beneath the surface of Lake Ontario, a layer of naturally cold water has become an unlikely part of Toronto’s urban infrastructure. Instead of relying entirely on conventional air-conditioning systems to cool its downtown buildings, the Canadian city uses the lake’s cold temperature as a source of cooling energy. According to a report by the Daily Commercial News, water drawn from about 83 metres below the surface was being used as part of a district cooling network serving buildings in Toronto’s downtown core. What started more than two decades ago has since grown into one of North America’s largest district energy systems. Today, the network serves around 200 buildings and more than 40 million square feet of downtown real estate, including offices, hospitals, hotels, condominiums, educational institutions and data centres.A 2004 cooling experimentToronto-based Enwave had begun using its Deep Lake Water Cooling (DLWC) system to cool buildings in the downtown core. The report explained that the system drew water from a permanently cold layer about 83 metres beneath Lake Ontario and described it as the largest renewable lake-source cooling system of its kind at the time. The project initially produced enough air conditioning to cool about 20 million square feet of office space. It was also reported to reduce electricity use by 75% compared with traditional air conditioning and was expected to eliminate about 40,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions.The key idea behind the system is that the water at the bottom of the lake remains cold enough to provide useful cooling even during Toronto’s hot summers. Rather than using the lake water directly inside buildings, Enwave uses its low temperature to transfer cooling energy into a separate water network.How lake water cools buildingsThe process begins deep in Lake Ontario, where cold water is drawn through intake pipes and sent to the Island Filtration Plant. The water is treated before reaching the John Street Pumping Station, where heat exchangers transfer its cooling energy to Enwave’s separate chilled-water system. This distinction is important: the lake water itself does not circulate through the buildings' air-conditioning systems. Instead, its cold temperature is used to cool another water loop. Heat exchangers transfer the cooling energy, creating chilled water that can then be distributed through underground pipes to connected buildings.Once inside a building, the chilled water absorbs heat from the building’s cooling system. The warmed water returns to the district system, where it can be cooled again and circulated back through the network. This centralised approach means individual buildings do not necessarily need to operate large conventional chiller plants of their own. Enwave says the system provides an alternative to traditional cooling towers and equipment, which can represent significant capital and operating costs for large buildings.A network that keeps growingThe system has expanded considerably since its launch. Enwave’s current information for Toronto states that its district energy network serves 200 buildings and more than 40 million square feet of downtown real estate. The network is supported by four interconnected downtown plants and about 25 miles (40 kilometres) of underground pipes. Its customers include hospitals, commercial offices, hotels, condominiums, institutions and data centres. The Deep Lake Water Cooling system remains the main anchor of the wider district-energy network. Some individual buildings have also benefited by no longer needing conventional cooling infrastructure. According to Enwave, Brookfield Place, which contains more than 2.6 million square feet of office space, eliminated the need for conventional chiller plants after connecting to the system.Turning nature into infrastructureToronto’s system demonstrates how a natural feature can become part of a city’s energy infrastructure. The cold water deep beneath Lake Ontario provides a stable source of cooling energy, while a centralised network distributes that cooling to hundreds of buildings. The system can reduce peak electricity-system generation compared with the demand that would otherwise be required by traditional cooling methods. That makes the concept particularly relevant for dense cities, where large numbers of buildings can place significant pressure on electricity systems during hot weather.More than 20 years after the original project began, Toronto’s Deep Lake Water Cooling system shows how district energy can move beyond individual building-by-building solutions. By using the naturally cold conditions deep within Lake Ontario and combining them with underground infrastructure and heat-exchange technology, the city has turned cold lake water into a large-scale cooling resource for its urban core.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Wales' Pisa test results fall further behind rest of UK
articles.summary: Three-yearly maths, reading and science test results show continued "downward trend", says OECD.
articles.body:
Wales' performance in international tests for 15-year-olds has fallen further behind other UK nations.

The biggest drop was in maths scores with reading results also lower, while average science scores in the three-yearly Pisa (Programme for International Student Assessment) study were slightly up.

The tests were taken by a sample of teenagers in 91 countries and economies in 2025, and are seen as an important yardstick of how education systems are performing.

When results were last published in 2023, Wales' recorded its lowest ever scores in all three subjects.

The minister for education and Welsh language, Anna Brychan, said plans were in place to support schools to raise standards.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) said the results showed Wales' "overall downward trend still continuing".

In Wales, 113 schools took part in Pisa with 3,406 pupils sitting the tests.

The average maths score fell from 466 to 456 while in other UK nations' results were broadly stable, leading to a widening gap as Wales fell further behind.

In every round of Pisa there is a focus on one of the three main test subjects and this time it was science - the only area where results were up a little.

Average scores increased from 473 in 2023 to 476 however improvements were greater in other nations with English teens hitting 516 - up 13 compared with three years earlier.

Welsh pupils' reading standards have been under scrutiny since the last set of Pisa results and scores fell again in the latest assessments, down from 466 to 459.

In the 2022 tests - the first after the pandemic - performance slumped in many nations but Welsh scores fell more steeply than the other UK nations.

It followed an uptick in the 2018 results.

Pupils at Ysgol Gyfun Gymraeg Glantaf in Cardiff took part in Pisa in 2025.

Caron, 16, said the test was different to usual assessments because they didn't revise for it and it was online rather than on paper "so that felt a bit weird".

"Depending on how you answered it it got easier or harder so it varied depending on how well you did."

Elin, 16, said: "Some of the questions were quite similar to what you might do in a science test, but some of the questions were quite random."

Unlike GCSEs, individual students don't get grades so Owain sad it "felt different".

"I don't think it was as serious," he said.

"When the questions got harder I backed out a bit, maybe gave a random answer."

Classmate Tiago said he enjoyed the experience of taking part in Pisa and knew that Wales had performed poorly in the past.

"Going in, I was excited because I really wanted to give it my all to boost the ranking," he said.

Headteacher Dyfrig Rees said it was important for schools to contribute to Pisa in order to give information about "how our teaching and learning compares to other countries".

He said it was one of a number of assessments for pupils doing their GCSEs.

"We do try and emphasise they should try their best, take their time and be focused but its secondary to other assessments in school life," he said.

He said he hoped Wales' new curriculum would ultimately lead to better results in Pisa.

"People are proud of the Welsh education sector, and they want it to be successful and so whenever there is a league table where we are not where we want to be -that's disappointing," he said.

More than 90 countries and economies took part in Pisa in 2025 with Asian countries and regions once again ranking highest including areas of China, Singapore and Japan.

But the UK featured in the top 10 for all three subjects and were described as "bucking the trend" of declining performance by the OECD.

However, Wales' performance was worse than England, Scotland and Northern Ireland and broadly in line with countries such as Spain and Croatia for both maths and science where it scored significantly below the average for OECD member countries.

For reading, it was on a par with Denmark and France and close to the OECD average.

In an extra test in this round of Pisa, Welsh teens also scored lower than their peers in other UK nations in computational problem solving.

Andreas Schleicher from the OECD said England had pursued "coherent and consistent policies in education" which were "conducive to producing good learning outcomes".

"That's not what we've seen in countries like Scotland or Wales to that extent," he added.

Though some of the decline in Welsh scores was not "statistically very robust" and science results had "stabilised", he said "unfortunately for Wales, we see that overall downward trend still continuing".

More than 760,000 students took the assessment in 91 countries and economies in 2025.

A sample of schools in each country are chosen to take part from which a representative sample of pupils are chosen.

Pupils are aged between 15 years, three months, and 16 years, two months - so usually in Year 11.

It's a two-hour online test and each student is tested in two subjects, getting different questions with variations in the combination and order of subjects.

There's also a background questionnaire which asks for information about the students, their homes and their school and learning experiences. School leaders also complete a questionnaire.

The OECD says Pisa "measures 15-year-olds' ability to use their reading, mathematics and science knowledge and skills to meet real-life challenges" and assesses the extent to which they have the tools "essential for full participation in social and economic life".

It claims results provide insight for governments on their competitiveness relative to other economies.

But some experts have questioned Pisa's value and the influence it has had in changing education policy.

After a big drop in the 2022 results the OECD said that "outcomes have largely stagnated or continued to decline in many countries".

Overall, the steepest decline was in reading displaying a long-term "weakening of performance" which predated the pandemic, the OECD said.

Schleicher said while "limited or moderate use" of digital devices for learning in school is often linked to better results, there were substantially worse outcomes when they were used for leisure in schools.

The OECD said key ways to improve education systems included having high and consistent expectations for pupils and to ensure teachers had strong teaching skills, not just subject knowledge, as well as using AI in a targeted way which did not replace "effortful learning".

Brychan reassured teachers and leaders that there would be no knee-jerk response to the results and plans were in place to support schools to raise standards.

"Let me be clear, these results are not where we want them to be. But in many ways, they reinforce what we knew already and highlight our need to improve standards of reading and maths, as a priority," she said.

Brychan said the Pisa results were not the only measure of performance and standards in schools, but that did not mean they should be "ignored", as "we take our performance in international studies incredibly seriously".

She added: "What matters now is what happens next and delivering on our promise to better support the education system to raise standards."

She said the Welsh government would be launching its Foundational Literacy and Numeracy Plan which represented an "important first step in the development of an equitable education system that works for all".

Helen Jenner MS, Reform UK Wales' shadow education minister, said the Pisa results are "stark and deeply concerning".

"We simply cannot go on with a situation where pupils in Wales are consistently falling behind their counterparts in other parts of the United Kingdom," she said.

Sam Rowlands MS, the Conservative shadow minister for education agreed that the gap with England is "stark", and added that this should be a "wake-up call" for the Welsh government.

"Every child in Wales deserves an education that gives them the best possible start in life," he said.

National Association of Head Teachers Cymru said the findings reinforce concerns about educational inequality and the growing pressures faced by schools supporting learners affected by poverty and poor wellbeing.

"School leaders need greater investment in staffing, support services, professional development and resources if they are to deliver the ambitions set out for Welsh education," said Dr Graham Gault, the NAHT national secretary.

"Raising standards requires sustained commitment and long-term planning, not constant policy change."

articles.title: Meet Linus Chen-Plotkin, the 18-year-old Philadelphia student who analysed more than 600 works by Mozart, Beethoven, Haydn, and Schubert and found Mozart's melodies were less predictable
articles.summary: US News: Mozart’s versatility is unparalleled, even today. Ever wondered what made him the ultimate musical architect, with every phrase perfectly placed and e.
articles.body: Mozart’s versatility is unparalleled, even today. Ever wondered what made him the ultimate musical architect, with every phrase perfectly placed and every note seemingly inevitable? Well, an 18-year-old from Philadelphia may have found the answer! Linus Chen-Plotkin analysed more than 600 classical compositions and discovered something that musicologists have debated for centuries but never quite quantified. Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s melodies are actually harder to predict than those of any other musician, including Beethoven and Schubert.Teen proves Mozart’s music is unpredictableFor his Regeneron Science Talent Search project, Linus built three statistical tests to measure something he calls a melody's ‘memory’. His project, ‘Predictability and Statistical Memory in Classical Sonatas and Quartets’, was to find out how much earlier notes influence the ones that come after. The ‘memory’ tracks how much one note depends on the notes before it. High memory means earlier phrases keep influencing what comes next, making it more predictable. Low memory means the composer pivots quickly, keeping listeners slightly off-balance.The teenager ran these tests across 600-plus piano sonatas and string quartets by Joseph Haydn, Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, Ludwig van Beethoven, and Franz Schubert. What he found was striking. Mozart's music had shorter memory across all three tests, which means his melodies broke patterns faster. They were less predictable. Mozart honoured classical form while constantly slipping something unexpected past the listener's ear. In other words, perfection in Mozart's case didn't mean predictability; it meant something far harder to achieve.Linus’ findings finally provide an answer to understanding Mozart's works. For centuries, critics have thrown around words like ‘genius’ and ‘innovation’ without pinning down what they mean. Linus gave us a way to climb closer to the answer. The unpredictability is what made Mozart the genius he was. An 18-year-old wrestler from Philadelphia picked up statistical tools and told us something new about how Mozart's mind worked. Perhaps Mozart would have enjoyed that twist.Meet Linus Chen-PlotkinBorn to Joshua Plotkin and Alice Chen-Plotkin, Linus hails from Philadelphia, PA. He is a student at the Germantown Friends School. He's a varsity wrestler and an advanced Mandarin student. He is not a classical music prodigy who spent his childhood at conservatories, but he knows its mathematics. During the statistical analysis, he approached classical music as a dataset. He saw centuries of musical tradition as raw material for mathematical investigation. He believes his approach and other quantitative methods can help improve the understanding of areas that are typically studied qualitatively. Think music theory, art history, and literature. All these fields have relied on interpretation for centuries, but Linus thinks they don't have to stay that way. Music is not really alien to him. In fact, he also sings and plays blues guitar at The Twisted Tail bourbon bar during his spare time. While he isn’t neck-deep in work, he doubles as a radio operator. Linus is also a licensed amateur radio operator and a former member and soloist of the Philadelphia Boys Choir & Chorale. Few people his age have taken so many different angles on the same art form!Beyond the projectLinus isn't stopping at the musical memory. He plans to go beyond. He's collaborating with a Johns Hopkins professor on analysing the grammatical rules of rhyme and metre in Geoffrey Chaucer's medieval poetry. He will be using the same approach on poems that belong to different centuries. The question is almost the same. Can we measure what makes great writing work? How does a poem resonate with the reader? What makes the best works the best?Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2015, NYC crews cut 11,000 love locks from the Brooklyn Bridge after their weight snapped a lamp wire; 2016 signs brought a $100 fine
articles.summary: US News: In 2015, NYC crews cut over 11,000 love locks from the Brooklyn Bridge due to safety concerns, prompting a crackdown that included signage warning of fines. The city urged couples to commemorate their love differently to preserve the iconic structure.
articles.body: New York City's Brooklyn Bridge had collected more than 11,000 so-called love locks in 2015, which was enough for city crews to spend thousands of hours removing the padlocks from the pedestrian promenade. Couples typically engraved their names or initials on the locks and attached them to the bridge as a symbol of their relationship.According to the New York City Department of Transportation, more than 11,000 locks were removed from the Brooklyn Bridge during 2015. The agency said its bridge crews conducted regular sweeps several times a year, which cost about $116,000 that year. City officials were concerned that the added weight and the objects attached to the bridge could damage infrastructure and create a hazard for vehicles below.A wire actually snappedOn September 8, 2016, a guy-wire that was connected to an overhead street lamp above Brooklyn-bound traffic snapped under the weight of dozens of love locks and other objects attached to it. The break forced the closure of a lane on the Brooklyn-bound roadway for about two hours while emergency crews made repairs. The incident was documented in the city's 2016 Bridges and Tunnels Annual Condition Report.Since the city began keeping count in 2013, more than 34,200 locks had been removed from the Brooklyn Bridge by the end of 2016. The city did not regard the locks as an isolated cosmetic problem since they were attached to cables, fences, railings and other parts of a structure that was carrying pedestrians above a busy roadway.The city started warning visitorsOn October 7, 2016, the Department of Transportation announced a coordinated effort to discourage visitors from leaving locks on the bridge. Crews removed hundreds of locks and other objects that day and installed signs warning visitors that attaching items to city property could result in a $100 fine. The signs used a crossed-out padlock and were placed along the pedestrian promenade.The city also contacted major travel-guide publishers, and asked them to discourage tourists from participating in the practice. The enforcement was based on a section of the city's Administrative Code that prohibits attaching objects to city property. The department said the practice had begun with only a few dozen locks in 2009 but had grown over the following years.The cleanup had become routineA 2015 Bridges and Tunnels report recorded 9,363 locks removed between January 1 and September 25 of that year. One April cleanup removed 450 locks weighing about 75 pounds in a single day, and these figures show why the city treated the locks as an ongoing maintenance issue rather than a one-time cleanup.The padlocks themselves were not especially heavy individually, as the problem came from their accumulation. Thousands of pieces of metal that are attached to bridge infrastructure added weight in places that were not intended to serve as storage points for personal objects. Visitors also began tying other items to the bridge, including hair bands, shoelaces and headphones.The policy was about the bridge, not the gestureThe city did not object to the romantic gesture itself, but its concern was where visitors were leaving the objects. In announcing the 2016 enforcement campaign, DOT officials asked visitors to find other ways to commemorate their relationships rather than attaching locks to the Brooklyn Bridge.Pedestrians use the upper promenade while traffic passes below, which means that maintenance work on the bridge can affect road users as well as visitors, and the September 2016 wire failure made that distinction concrete.The practice had begun with a few dozen locks that had developed into a recurring maintenance operation involving thousands of pieces of metal and, in at least one case, enough weight to break a wire supporting a street lamp. By October 2016, the city's response was no longer limited to cutting off the locks; it included warning signs, enforcement and requests that travel guides help change visitor behavior.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: How China's exercise with Egypt made the IAF better suited to take on the dragon
articles.summary: News News: When China sent its J-16 'Hidden Dragon' fighters to Egypt for Exercise Eagles of Civilisation, the headline takeaway was straightforward, Beijing's p.
articles.body: When China sent its J-16 'Hidden Dragon' fighters to Egypt for Exercise Eagles of Civilisation, the headline takeaway was straightforward, Beijing's pilots finally got a close look at the Rafale, the same jet that forms the backbone of India's own fighter fleet. But a closer look at what actually happened suggests the exercise may have done India's air force more favours than China's.The Indian Air Force currently operates 36 Rafales, with 114 more in the pipeline, and until a fifth-generation stealth fighter enters service, this 4.5-generation aircraft remains India's most potent platform. What sets the Rafale apart, beyond stealth shaping it lacks, is its advanced sensor fusion, network centricity and supercruise capability, features that put it firmly in fifth-generation territory in most respects but one. Its "omnirole" design philosophy lets a single aircraft strike, self-escort, designate targets with lasers, run electronic warfare through its SPECTRA suite, and conduct battle damage assessment, all within one mission, even though real-world operations typically split these roles across multiple aircraft.This is precisely where the Egypt exercise becomes useful for India rather than China. Every time a Rafale's SPECTRA system encounters a hostile radar, in this case the J-16's AESA radar, it logs that signature into its threat library, effectively building institutional knowledge across the entire global Rafale fleet, India included. In other words, China's own jets unwittingly handed India's defence planners fresh data on how to detect and counter the J-16 in a future conflict.That said, caution is warranted before drawing sweeping conclusions. Egypt's Rafales differ meaningfully from India's in weapons, sensors, software and operational doctrine, meaning this exercise cannot be read as a proxy for an actual India-China air battle. The most consequential gap is the missing Meteor missile, the Rafale's signature long-range BVR weapon, which Egypt's jets don't carry. Without it, Egyptian pilots are unlikely to have developed genuine long-range BVR tactics against the Meteor's engagement envelope, meaning the PLA Air Force's exposure here offers limited insight into countering India's actual Rafale loadout. China has had somewhat better exposure elsewhere, having exercised against Thailand's Gripens, which do carry the Meteor, but that remains a different airframe altogether.

articles.title: "Si lo de Rodri lo hace Vinicius, no hay telediarios en el mundo para comentarlo"
articles.standfirst: La Tribu analiza el comentario de Rodri en el banquillo de Mestalla sobre el nivel del Valencia
articles.summary: La Tribu analiza el comentario de Rodri en el banquillo de Mestalla sobre el nivel del Valencia
articles.body: José Luis Sánchez, Ricardo Rosety, Pablo Pinto, Jorge Segura, Ricardo Sierra y José Luis Allegue han sido los tertulianos de este viernes en La Tribu, patrocinada por Sportium durante esta temporada, para analizar la comparecencia de Mbappé en la previa del Real Madrid-Inter de Champions y las palabras de Rodri en el banquillo de Mestalla criticando el nivel del Valencia. Raúl Varela fue especialmente crítico con el capitán de España y puso sobre la mesa una comparación con Vinicius: "Si lo que hace Rodri lo hace Vinicius, no hay telediarios en el mundo para comentarlo...". "Lo ocurrido con Rodri es de falta de compañerismo y de tacto, falta de elegancia. Es el capitán de España. Si eso lo llega a decir Cristiano, faltan periódicos para titular hoy. Si eso lo llega a decir Cristiano no vuelve a pisar Valencia", aseguró Raúl Varela. El presentador de La Tribu puso especial énfasis en el contexto en el que se produjo el comentario de Rodri: "Un segundo antes de haber hecho ese feo comentario, Mestalla aplaudió a Rodri por ser campeón del mundo. Me parece más hiriente decirlo en el banquillo. Lo hace en un ambiente relajado y sincero, en un partido resuelto y después de recibir una ovación cariñosa del público, sin provocación ni incitación". José Luis Sánchez también se mostró muy crítico: "Es un error tremendo y una falta de compañerismo. Por más vueltas que se dé, por más protección que se le quiera dar, Rodri no es un canterano, sabe lo que es LaLiga, el fútbol español, las retransmisiones españolas, y le han cazado en una falta de respeto a los compañeros, no tiene defensa". Además, añadió: "En el City también le sancionaron por un menosprecio a un rival, o sea que no es la primera vez". Ricardo Sierra aportó otra visión del episodio: "Rodri viene de Inglaterra, no se acuerda de que hay cámaras que le están mirando y lo hace sin ningún tipo de filtro. Es un comentario futbolístico desacertado, entiendo que pueda ofender a algún valencianista, pero estoy seguro de que mucha gente del fútbol lo entiende. Este tipo de comentarios se suelen hacer en un contexto privado", añadió. Ricardo Rosety diferenció entre hacer ese comentario en el banquillo y dirigirse directamente a un adversario: "Una cosa es decirlo en el banquillo, que es feo, y otra es decírselo en la cara al rival, que es aún más feo". José Luis Allegue sostuvo precisamente la postura contraria: "Es un comentario feo, desafortunado. Me parece más honesto decírselo a un rival que decirlo en el banquillo". Pablo Pinto defendió que no se pueden equiparar ambas situaciones: "No tiene nada que ver una conversación privada captada por unas cámaras que ir a provocar a un rival o afición rival. Lo que opina Rodri lo opinan los 45.000 valencianistas que había en la grada de Mestalla. No está diciendo ninguna barbaridad". Jorge Segura también rechazó la comparación con una provocación directa: "No se puede comparar lo de Rodri con que un tío se gire a la grada y les diga 'a Segunda, a Segunda', o con que un jugador se encare con otro y le diga 'eres muy malo, tú quién eres'. En el Madrid ha picado mucho que Rodri se fuera al Barça".

articles.title: Singapore: Highest paid world leader Lawrence Wong to get salary increase of $1 million
articles.summary: Singapore's prime minister Lawrence Wong will see his annual pay rise to 3.6 million Singapore dollars ($2.8m; £2.1m).
articles.body:
Singapore's government says it will raise the annual salaries of its ministers and other office holders, including its prime minister who is the highest paid political leader in the world.

Lawrence Wong will see an increase of 1.4 million Singapore dollars ($1.1m; £818,000) in his annual pay package. He has said he will donate this pay increase to charity over the next five years.

Wong said that raising the pay of ministers was necessary to attract better talent. The government has previously argued that paying ministers high salaries deters corruption.

But the move has attracted criticism in Singapore where there is deep concern about job security and the rising cost of living.

Even before his pay raise kicks in, Wong is still by far the highest paid world leader.

He currently receives an annual salary of S$2.2m and will now see his pay go up by more than 60% to S$3.6m ($2.8m).

Next is Hong Kong chief executive John Lee, who earns about $719,000, followed by Switzerland's president Guy Parmelin with $606,000.

US president Donald Trump earns $400,000 a year, while British PM Andy Burnham takes in $230,000.

On Tuesday, Wong acknowledged that Singapore ministers' salaries have attracted scrutiny given that they were much more than what most citizens earn. The median monthly income in the country is S$5,775.

But he argued that he has faced difficulty convincing business leaders and top civil servants to run for political office.

While the government cannot match what some of these people earn, "we do not make the financial hurdle unnecessarily high" for them to give up their careers and join politics, he said.

"Overall, I believe this will give me and future prime ministers a better chance of persuading capable Singaporeans to step forward, and of building the strongest possible team for Singapore," he said.

Currently, the base pay package of ministers is about S$1.1m. With the new pay scheme, that will increase to around S$1.2m.

But Wong said he expects most of these ministers to receive even more than that - around S$1.35m - by the end of the current term of government, as pay will increase based on performance.

Part of their pay package is determined by whether the country reaches certain targets for unemployment rate, income growth, and GDP growth.

The topic of high salaries for Singapore's ministers has long been a lightning rod of criticism for the ruling People's Action Party (PAP), which has led the country since independence.

In a landmark general election in 2011 the PAP saw its lowest vote share in decades, fuelled partly by voters' unhappiness over ministers' pay as well as immigration policies. The following year, the government slashed ministers' salaries.

Wong's predecessor, Lee Hsien Loong, had also pledged to donate his salary increase to charity for several years back in 2007.

The government has for years pointed to its lack of corruption - Singapore consistently ranks near the top of Transparency International's annual Corruption Perceptions Index - as proof that the ministerial pay system works, arguing that it reduces the temptation for ministers to accept bribes.

But in a country where the average income is far below such sums, the issue continues to rankle and the latest announcement is no exception.

On Tuesday many online posted comments critical of the pay raise, saying it was "tone deaf" given current concerns about retrenchments, jobs for fresh graduates and inflation.

Retrenchments in Singapore hit their highest level in more than five years in the last quarter, according to government figures.

But there were a few who agreed with the move, saying it was necessary to have "the best of the best" running the country.

articles.title: Uber's layoff memo also has a work from home message for the remaining 29,000 employees: We're establishing clearer principles for where roles and teams should...
articles.summary: Tech News News: Uber's memo to staff on Wednesday cut about 3,300 jobs, but the line that changes daily life for everyone still employed is the one about working from.
articles.body: Uber's memo to staff on Wednesday cut about 3,300 jobs, but the line that changes daily life for everyone still employed is the one about working from home. The company is ending remote work as a normal way to work at Uber. Fully remote roles will be capped at roughly 1% of the workforce, down from a share built up over five years of hiring people wherever they happened to live.Everyone else who works from home is being asked to move to an office. The three-day-a-week hybrid policy stays, and Uber says it will keep pushing for compliance with it. For a company that will have just under 30,000 employees once the cuts are done, that turns a layoff announcement into a relocation notice for a large part of the staff it is keeping.Only 1% of Uber employees will still be allowed to work from homeThat 1% is the number to hold on to. It is not a target or a preference, it is a ceiling, and it applies globally. Chief executive Dara Khosrowshahi framed the reversal around what he said Uber has learned since the pandemic, that sitting together and solving problems in person works better than the alternative. The memo says Uber is "asking the vast majority of remote employees to move to an office", which is a polite way of saying the job now comes with a postcode.Uber's return-to-office plan ties decide where employees have to liveThe company has drawn up rules for where each kind of team belongs. Global teams go to New York and San Francisco. Regional teams go to designated regional hubs, local teams to country hubs, and engineering to tech hubs. Managers will be placed with their own teams wherever Uber can manage it, and early-career employees are singled out as the group that should not be sitting alone. Uber has not said which offices are worst hit by the job cuts, so people in smaller locations are dealing with two questions at once, whether their role survives and whether it survives in the city they live in.Uber will start counting who shows up three days a weekPlenty of companies have a hybrid policy on paper that nobody counts. Uber is saying it will count. Three days a week in the office remains the standard, and the memo commits to reinforcing compliance rather than leaving it to managers. Read alongside the hub consolidation, that is what makes the move harder than a typical return-to-office push. Attendance is measured against a specific building, and Uber has decided which building that is.The job cuts and the robotaxi bet sit behind the office orderThe layoffs themselves are about flattening. Uber has cut the number of employees sitting seven or more layers below the CEO by 20% and halved the number of teams with only one or two direct reports. Three delivery operations teams covering restaurants, retail and direct commerce are merging, and in engineering, Core Services Engineering and Science are being combined.Khosrowshahi said revenue has nearly tripled in five years and left behind layers, coordination and unclear ownership. He did not blame artificial intelligence, which sets this apart from most technology layoffs this year. The pressure is competitive. Waymo runs through Uber's app in Austin and Atlanta while expanding elsewhere on its own, Tesla is pushing driverless rides, and Uber plans to spend more than $10 billion to stay the marketplace those cars plug into. Analysts estimate annual savings of up to $2 billion.Uber said everyone affected by the job cuts has already been told. It has not said the same about the remote employees now expected to relocate.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: For 100 years, Milwaukee has been turning human waste into lawn fertiliser; 10.5 billion pounds diverted from landfills
articles.summary: US News: A century-old Milwaukee process transforms human waste into a bestselling lawn fertiliser, turning a disposal problem into a circular economy. This ha.
articles.body: A century-old Milwaukee process transforms human waste into a bestselling lawn fertiliser, turning a disposal problem into a circular economy. This has saved over 10 billion pounds of waste from going to a landfill and being packaged into bags of lawn fertiliser. The waste that the city flushes away is sold to people who want a greener and healthier yard. The acting agent in the middle is a colony of microbes that ate the waste and then died.Milorganite: From waste to fertiliserThe product's name is Milorganite and Milwaukee's city sewer district has been making it since the 1920s. The name is a mashup of Milwaukee Organic Nitrogen. It is a slow-release fertiliser made by the Milwaukee Metropolitan Sewerage District and it comes out of the process of cleaning the city's wastewater. The production began in 1926, with the first railcar shipping on February 10. The plant for the process is located at the Jones Island facility and Milorganite calls it the world's first large-scale plant of its kind.The backbone of the entire thing is biology and not some extravagant machinery. Naturally occurring microbes are added to the incoming wastewater, where they feed on the nutrients dissolved in it. As they eat, they clean the water. Peter Coffaro, the district’s director of public engagement, put it plainly: “They are eating the material. It’s a short and happy life. They are eating a lot and they are reproducing.”Once the microbes run out of food, they die off. The cleaned water is disinfected and returned to Lake Michigan. Now, what is left behind is a mass of dead microbes which serves as raw material. The water is taken out of the mass and converted into a dry, stable material, safe to bag and sell.“In most treatment plant processes, it’s always about needing to remove that water and get that waste off, and generally it goes to landfill, and we are able to recycle that product,” said Coffaro.According to the maker, the dead microbes are dried in high-temperature rotating kilns “heated to 900–1200 ⁰F to kill pathogens and form pellets.” That temperature is the safety step. It turns a wet, biologically active sludge into a dry pellet that can sit in a garage.What comes out is a slow-release nitrogen product that the maker says feeds plants over about 8-10 weeks, which is the selling point for gardeners who don’t want a fast green burst followed by a crash. Nearly a hundred years later, the district serves over 1 million customers in 29 communities.Saving space in landfillsHow does this help? Milorganite's own history page puts the running total at over 10.5 billion pounds. The National Association of Clean Water Agencies, which gave the district an award, similarly credited it with having “diverted over ten billion pounds of nutrient-rich fertiliser pellets to residential, professional, and agricultural markets.”The entire process transforms the idea of "waste." A landfill treats leftover solids as the endpoint, something to be buried and forgotten. But Milwaukee treats the same material as inventory. The microbes first clean the water, then become a product that enriches lawns and farms, eventually saving the city loads of cash it would shell to throw the waste away. Moreover, what makes the Milwaukee process even more vital is that it has been going on for a century, substantiating its worth.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: “Read first, then watch TV”: Soha Ali Khan says sometimes you have to ‘bribe your children’, but warns against a common parenting mistake
articles.summary: Getting a child to pick up a book when there is a television, tablet or phone waiting nearby is hardly an easy parenting battle. Soha Ali Khan knows t.
articles.body: Getting a child to pick up a book when there is a television, tablet or phone waiting nearby is hardly an easy parenting battle. Soha Ali Khan knows this well. The actor and mother to daughter Inaaya Naumi Kemmu has admitted that sometimes, getting children to develop a habit they don't naturally enjoy requires a little negotiation- and even a little bribery.In an interview with Tweak India, Soha talked about her parenting approach and said she sometimes tells her daughter, “Inaaya, until you read this book, you can't watch TV.” And she is quite candid about the fact that this is not necessarily a perfect or foolproof strategy.“Sometimes you have to bribe your children, sometimes you have to incentivise them,” Soha said, acknowledging that not every child will automatically grow up loving books.‘Not all of them will be born readers’For Soha, one of the biggest parenting traps is comparing your child with another child who seems to be doing something effortlessly.She admitted that she has friends whose children are naturally enthusiastic readers and that, as a mother, she has also wondered why her daughter cannot be more like them.But telling a child to become like someone else, she pointed out, can have the opposite effect. “I have a lot of friends who have children who are readers and I'm like, my God, how do I tell Inaya, why can't you be more like X, Y and Z?” she said.And she knows exactly why that approach does not work. “Of course I do. Does it work? No, of course not,” Soha said, explaining that the moment children are compared with someone else, they can “completely rebel and revolt”.Instead of motivating them, the comparison can become another reason for them to resist the very behaviour parents are trying to encourage.Her bigger lesson: Children copy what they seeFor Soha, the more important question is not simply how to make a child read a book. It is what the child sees the adults doing every day. “You set an example by being a good role model,” she said.That means parents cannot spend the entire evening scrolling on their phones and then expect their children to happily put away their screens and read. Soha's own advice is simple: “You don't be on your phone all the time and then suggest they read a book.”Instead, she believes books need to become part of the child's surroundings. “You read books around them, you leave books around them,” she said. It is a small distinction, but an important one. Rather than presenting reading as yet another rule imposed by adults, parents can make it something children regularly see and experience at home.Soha does not pretend parenting always works perfectlyWhat makes Soha's approach relatable is that she does not present parenting as a perfectly executed formula. She openly acknowledges that incentives may sometimes be necessary and that even comparisons can creep into a parent's mind. But she also recognises when a strategy is likely to backfire.Her approach appears to be less about forcing Inaaya to become “a reader” overnight and more about creating an environment where reading has a place alongside television and other forms of entertainment.In fact, Soha's comments fit with the parenting philosophy she has spoken about elsewhere: she sets boundaries for her daughter, but also understands that consistency has to come from the adults at home. In a recent interview, she spoke about her non-negotiable 8 pm bedtime for Inaaya and said she tries to maintain a schedule because routine is important for a child.Perhaps the most interesting part of Soha's parenting lesson is that she does not suggest banning television altogether or assuming that every child will naturally love books. Instead, there can be room for both- with some boundaries.A child may need an incentive to pick up a book initially. But if reading is never seen at home, a lecture about its importance may have limited impact. Soha's message to parents is therefore less about finding the perfect reward and more about looking at their own habits. Because sometimes, the parenting lesson a child absorbs is not the one a parent says out loud- it is the one they watch every day.Looking for trusted parenting advice? articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Union minister Kiren Rijiju on Tuesday slammed Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi for \"politicising\" the killing of Manipuri music.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Union minister Kiren Rijiju on Tuesday slammed Lok Sabha leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi for "politicising" the killing of Manipuri musician C Vikram Singh in Delhi, saying that the focus should be on immediate action.While talking to reporters, Rijiju said that Rahul should not bring BJP into the issue and said that Delhi Police takes immediate action whenever an incident involving people from the North East occurs."This is not the time for politics. I keep asking why Rahul Gandhi brings the BJP into this? When an incident occurs—a tragedy resulting in someone's death—the focus should be on immediate action. This is not a matter for politics," Rijiju said."The North East Special Police Cell established within the Delhi Police remains in constant contact, ensuring immediate action in the event of any incident. Things are no longer as they used to be; we have put a system in place to take swift measures. Consequently, whenever an incident involving people from the North East occurs in Delhi, immediate action is taken," he added.This comes after Rahul condemned the death of Manipuri musician Chongtham Vikram Singh, who was allegedly assaulted by a group of men and questioned Union home minister Amit Shah and Delhi Police over what they were doing to stop the "growing lawlessness" against people from the Northeast in Delhi."Chongtham Vikram Singh ji, a renowned musician from Manipur, went downstairs to ask some men to lower the noise outside his home. He was beaten to death for it. A father, killed outside his own home, in his own country's capital. After many such incidents, every Northeast family in Delhi is asking the same question today - are we safe here?" the Congress leader said."What are Shah's MHA and Delhi Police doing to stop this growing lawlessness, especially against people from the Northeast? There must be a swift investigation, and the culprits must be brought to justice. My condolences to Vikram ji's family," he added.The 54-year-old Manipuri music teacher allegedly died after being assaulted by a group of men in Kilokari Village, in Delhi’s Ashram area, following a dispute over noise and nuisance outside his residence.According to police, Vikram Singh had objected to alleged shouting and nuisance by delivery boys and dhaba staff opposite his house. When he came downstairs to object, he was allegedly attacked with fists and blows.Vikram was taken to Holy Family Hospital by his son Yaiphaba for treatment, where he later succumbed to his injuries.According to the Police, a PCR call regarding the alleged beating of C Vikram Singh was received at Delhi's Sunlight Colony police station on September 7. When he came downstairs and objected, he was allegedly assaulted with fists and blows.The official further informed that they have registered an FIR under murder provisions and said all the accused, including minors, have been apprehended.Further investigation is still under way.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Public opposed to disability benefit cuts, major survey suggests
articles.summary: Around 7% of those polled wanted disability benefit cuts, according to the latest British social attitudes survey.
articles.body:
Amid widespread political concern about the rising cost of disability benefits, a new survey suggests the public does not support cutting the payments.

Research by the British social attitudes survey found 7% of respondents were in favour of reducing benefits for disabled people who cannot work.

Almost half of those who took part, 49%, said they supported more being spent on disability benefits, even if it led to higher taxes.

The findings come despite the proportion of those who support increasing welfare spending for the poor being at a near record low.

Labour, the Conservative party and Reform UK have all said there is a need to reduce the amount of money being spent on health and disability benefits, while the Liberal Democrats, Greens and SNP oppose reductions.

Efforts by Sir Keir Starmer to introduce cuts last year were opposed by many in his own party, forcing a government climbdown .

The proportion of GDP the UK spends on all welfare benefits for those of working age has remained broadly flat over the past 40 years, at just under 5%.

It has occasionally increased to over 5%, including in the 1990s, after the financial crisis in 2008, and during the Covid pandemic.

Despite that, the survey found that support for increasing welfare payments to help the poor was close to the lowest level the researchers have ever recorded.

Asked if "the government should spend more money on welfare benefits for the poor, even if it leads to higher taxes," 27% replied they should while 42% were opposed.

While wider welfare spending has, proportionately, remained stable, payments for disability benefits have taken up an increasing share of the total.

The latest figures show four million people in England and Wales are currently in receipt of Personal Independence Payment (PIP), the main disability benefit.

Annual spending has increased sharply from £16.3bn in 2019/20 to £27.3bn in 2024/25, and is forecast to rise to more than £41bn by 2030.

But around half of those polled for the survey supported higher spending on disability benefits overall, while a majority also strongly backed extra payments for the costs of having a disability.

Around 83% of respondents supported additional payments to help with cooking, 80% for budgeting, and 78% for washing.

Just 3% replied that "nobody should get any additional money" for all three tasks.

Respondents were not asked if they thought it should be harder to claim those benefits.

"Despite growing political divisions on welfare, support for disability benefits remains remarkably strong," said Dr Robert de Vries from the University of Kent, who was one of the report's co-authors.

"Very few people favour cuts, disabled people are seen as among the most deserving recipients of support, and proposals to reduce disability benefits appear politically risky across the political spectrum."

Proposals to reform PIP are due to be unveiled by the government in the autumn after an interim report published in the summer found the benefit was not fit for purpose .

Around 57% of Labour voters polled for the survey favoured more spending on disability benefits.

But there was broad political consensus that cuts would be wrong – just 5% of Labour voters, 7% of Conservatives and 11% of Reform UK backers said they supported cuts to those payments.

The British social attitude survey, carried out by the National Centre for Social Research, has been gauging public opinion since 1983.

Its latest survey saw 4,656 interviews gathered between August and October 2025.

The authors noted that the timing of the interviews, just after the Starmer government had failed to reform PIP, meant it was "possible that people were particularly supportive of disability benefits at the time".

They cautioned that public attitudes to disability benefits "crucially depend on which disabled people are in the public's mind", referencing previous research which showed that "some types of disabled people are seen as 'deserving' by the public".

articles.title: In 2013, a South Carolina marine professor collected over 100 tonnes of restaurant oyster shells for reefs; within one year, about 100 metres had functioning habitat
articles.summary: US News: Discover how Dr. Loren Coen's initiative to recycle restaurant oyster shells is revitalizing South Carolina's marine ecosystems and creating functional habitats within just one year.
articles.body: Oyster reefs once spread so widely across South Carolina's coastal marshes that early explorers reported entire creek banks covered in shell. Since free-swimming oyster larvae can only attach themselves to hard surfaces and the reefs' own discarded shells were historically the best surface of all, decades of fishing eliminated both the oysters and the very substance that future generations of oysters must settle on. Reef rehabilitation has increasingly looked to recycled oyster shells from restaurants as a practical source of hard substrate when other shell supplies are limited.A marine scientist with a habit of counting shellsDr. Keith Walters has spent much of his career working on oyster reef ecology and restoration. A marine science professor at Coastal Carolina University, Walters led the Coastal Oyster Recycling and Restoration Initiative (CORRI), which began in 2013 to recycle oyster shells from restaurants, build new reefs, and evaluate how those reefs functioned as habitat. His restoration work included constructing reefs from recycled shell across six South Carolina estuaries and monitoring the resulting oyster and fish communities.In 2013, Coen transformed that research focus into a practical collection effort, working with eateries to collect their leftover oyster shells instead of throwing them in the garbage and using the bagged shells to construct new reef structures along the coast of South Carolina. Over the course of the effort, he and his partners claim to have collected over 100 tonnes of restaurant shell. This is a significant harvest for a single season in a state where restaurants and shucking houses continue to discard significantly more shell than is recycled annually.Why the shell itself is the hard partThat shortage explains why Coen's restaurant partnership mattered so much. According to the South Carolina Sea Grant Consortium, less than 10 per cent of the oyster shell available for recycling in the state was being returned to the water, forcing the state’s own restoration programs to buy shell from out-of-state processors just to keep up with demand. Volunteers haul out bagged shells and load them onto barges or stack them in intertidal areas chosen for their tidal flow and existing colonies of oyster larvae, because a reef erected in the wrong place would simply wash away or lie unused no matter how much shell is put into it.The resulting reef then had to be monitored to determine whether it developed into functioning habitat rather than simply remaining a pile of shell. Generally, government-run schemes collect shells from public drop-off sites and a rotating list of restaurant partners, then quarantine them for months before they are safe to return to the water, reducing the risk of transferring illness to wild oyster populations.For restoration standards, a quick outcomeBy that measure, Walters' 2013 reefs fared well. Within one year of construction, the restored habitat was functioning as a refuge for reef-associated species across roughly 100 metres of shoreline, supporting a species assemblage that researchers would ordinarily expect only after several years of natural reef development. Reef development studies carried out through the South Carolina Department of Natural Resources have focused specifically on measuring these functional characteristics, tracking how quickly a bare shell structure begins supporting the fish, crabs and other species that make a reef ecologically useful rather than merely present.In a restoration field where results are measured in half decades, not months, a reef that reached that stage within twelve months was remarkable enough to be cited as evidence that restaurant shell, arriving in inconsistent batches and requiring lengthy quarantine before use, can build reef structure just as effectively as shell sourced in any other way. The project demonstrated that recycled restaurant shells could be collected, quarantined, bagged and used to construct functioning oyster habitat.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
